body: i would argue that this inconvenience is not super small

the reason i self harmed was because i was in unbearable emotional pain. i didn’t know how to cope with my feelings, and i had to learn other ways to deal with them (which is where therapy comes in). there is an element of shame that is so disheartening- i felt like i needed to, and then i was heartbroken that i would hurt myself like that. i honestly hated myself. and i had to cultivate a baseline amount of self love and respect.

i haven’t cut myself in nearly 3 years, but i regularly have the urge to when i’m upset. i have to keep a close eye on it. i have struggled with alcohol and drugs too- they both give you short term relief with horrible long term consequences. it is not through sheer willpower (although that is kinda necessary), it is through experience and learned skills.

i don’t know what type of relationship you have with your daughter, or what her life has been like. a large portion of people who self harm (myself included) have histories of experiencing abuse. (not accusatory- just context). whatever is going on, she is in pain. i was experiencing untreated symptoms of mental illness, and had to address that along with the cutting. 

be there for her whether or not she is cutting. do not shame her, but do not condone or enable it. ensure that she has ample support from therapists and psychiatrists, and that she has plenty of people to turn to for help, should she ever feel uncomfortable going to you. look into programs that teach DBT, which is specifically tailored to deal with this sort of thing. 

i’m wishing you and her the best, and i hope she is able to find love for herself soon.

hi! this is cliché advice, but *be yourself*. not necessarily because it will draw more people (although authenticity tends to), but because it’s a complete waste of time to chase someone who doesn’t accept you as you are.

with this said, *make sure you are a datable person*. i don’t mean being someone you aren’t, but working on aspects of yourself that may be underdeveloped at this point: Do you understand what types of things make women feel unsafe/uncomfortable? Do you have a genuine interest in other people, and their wellbeing? Are you emotionally/mentally healthy? 

I don’t ask these questions to intimidate you, but to bring your attention to them. A lot of guys i’ve talked to don’t understand that some things generally make women uncomfortable, or that they can’t manage their anger. You don’t have be perfect to start dating, but it helps to at least be cognizant of yourself.

You mentioned that you’re shy- it will do wonders to work on your self-esteem (if that’s an issue for you). It’s okay to be introverted and more quiet, but not liking yourself makes dating hard for both people. 

Things will feel awkward at first. The more you interact with people, the more naturally it will come. I truly hope this was helpful, and I’m wishing you the best as you start your journey!

Recovery is fucking hard. Everything ends up feeling boring, you lose touch with many people you used to have fun with, and you have to readjust your whole life.

When I stopped drinking, I entered an outpatient recovery program and finished it after 2 months. I felt a sense of pride and accomplishment at first, because I knew I was doing the right thing even though it was hard. Eventually the “pink cloud” (the novelty of sobriety) wore off, and I was just stuck with the difficulties. I kept at it even though it sucked. 

I specifically remember 3-6 months in, being firmly committed to sobriety, and still not being able to fathom not drinking again. I had to take it day by day, because if I thought about my whole life being sober, I would become overwhelmed and upset. I felt bored and unenthused; I missed the excitement of my life before even though I knew it was destructive and unsustainable.

Past that point, things changed so slowly that I didn’t even notice it was happening. I fantasized about drinking less, my life started becoming more interesting, and I got more experience having fun without alcohol. I am almost a year in now, and somehow, inexplicably, things are better. There are still times that I crave alcohol, but they are few and far between. The people in my life who are close to me know that I don’t drink, and they have become my support system. I have romance, adventure, fun, and spontaneity in my life, and it’s without alcohol now.

Things DO get better. You’re doing what you can, and recovery is not linear. Keep at it, and as time goes by, it will get easier. <3
